quirks.summary: The write demands an integrity claim on the body, so a request with neither Content-MD5 nor an x-amz-checksum header is refused with 400 before the document is parsed.

evidence.summary: The request documents Content-MD5 as the base64 digest of the configuration, which the pinned model spells as a request checksum requirement.

quirks.summary: Unknown elements inside the request document are skipped rather than refused — and the stakes are higher here than in any sibling family, because RustFS parses the stored replication document fail-closed: a decoder that got stricter on the next release would not silently switch replication off, it would make the bucket unusable.

evidence.summary: AWS ignores unknown elements in request XML, and upstream had to relax its decoder to match after strict parsing broke real clients.
The upstream fix that makes unknown request elements a skip rather than an error, which is the behaviour this decoder generates by construction.

quirks.summary: A rule is either V2 — a Filter, which then demands Priority and DeleteMarkerReplication beside it — or V1 — a bare rule-level Prefix, which carries neither; a rule mixing the two schema versions is refused with 400 InvalidRequest, because the version of a stored configuration is decided by exactly this distinction.

evidence.summary: The operation documents that a configuration adding the Filter element must also add DeleteMarkerReplication, Status and Priority.

The backward-compatibility section defines V2 as the format whose rules carry Filter and V1 as the format whose rules carry a direct Prefix child, with delete-marker handling implicit in V1 rather than spelled.

quirks.summary: A Filter takes at most one direct child — Prefix, Tag or And — and several conditions must nest inside one And, which exists only to combine and therefore needs at least two; two direct siblings are refused as MalformedXML. An empty Filter passes: it is the documented spelling for a rule that applies to every object.

evidence.summary: The type documents that a Filter must specify exactly one Prefix, Tag or And child element, and that combined conditions are wrapped in an And.
The filter walkthrough shows an empty Filter applying the rule to all objects, and every multi-condition example wrapped in a single And.

quirks.summary: A rule ID is bounded at 255 characters and must be unique within the configuration, and the document as a whole is bounded at 1000 rules; an ID over the cap or duplicated is refused with 400 InvalidArgument, the rule-count overflow with 400 InvalidRequest.

evidence.summary: The ID member is documented as a unique identifier for the rule with a maximum of 255 characters.
The guide documents the per-bucket cap of 1000 replication rules and states the limit is not adjustable.

quirks.summary: Two rules carrying the same Priority are stored and echoed rather than refused: AWS documents no uniqueness requirement, only how the engine resolves a conflict between overlapping rules by taking the highest number — so refusing duplicates would invent a rule a stored document could already be breaking, under the one configuration RustFS parses fail-closed.

evidence.summary: The Priority member documents only precedence between conflicting rules — the higher number wins — and states no uniqueness constraint the codec could enforce.

quirks.summary: The replica KMS key id and the destination account id are configuration secrets: the stored document echoes them on the read — that is the documented GET behaviour — but every refusal message is a constant that never carries them, so a rejected write cannot leak a key id or an account id into an error body or a log line.

evidence.summary: The documented response echoes the stored destination configuration including the ReplicaKmsKeyID and Account members, which pins the echo as read behaviour rather than error behaviour.
Upstream's secret-handling fixes are the record of how easily key material reaches unintended surfaces once it is carried as a plain string.

quirks.summary: The destination Bucket member is typed as a bucket name in the model but carries an ARN on the wire — arn:aws:s3:::bucket — so it is decoded as a plain string and neither the bucket-name grammar nor any ARN grammar is enforced on it: the model's type is unenforceable and a stricter grammar would be this project's invention.

evidence.summary: The Bucket member is documented as the Amazon Resource Name of the destination bucket, a value the S3 bucket-name grammar itself would refuse.

quirks.summary: A Status outside the documented Enabled/Disabled pair is stored and echoed rather than refused: the stored document is re-parsed by every future release, RustFS parses this one configuration fail-closed, and a spelling refused tomorrow that was accepted yesterday would make the bucket unusable rather than merely switch a feature off.

evidence.summary: The Status member documents Enabled and Disabled as its value set; passing out-of-set spellings through is this project's recorded fail-open decision.
Upstream's replication configuration types could not round-trip stored documents, the failure a strict enum decode reintroduces.

quirks.summary: The x-amz-bucket-object-lock-token request header is parsed into the input and passed through to the backend untouched: whether the token actually permits enabling Object Lock on the source bucket is the storage backend's semantic question, and the codec neither requires nor validates the header.

evidence.summary: The request documents the optional x-amz-bucket-object-lock-token header as a token allowing Object Lock to be enabled for an existing bucket.

quirks.summary: A syntactically non-empty Filter whose children are all unknown is refused before decoding can collapse it to the explicit empty Filter that means every object; an empty Filter and a known condition beside unknown children remain accepted.

evidence.summary: A lower-case Prefix or unknown wrapper was observed to decode as an empty filter, silently widening a scoped replication rule to every object.
